records.title: Connected and Eager to Learn: Digital Skills, Challenges, and Unmet Needs of Older Adults in Long-Term Care Facilities
records.abstract: This study explores the digital skills and challenges of older adults living in long-term care settings. We conducted 14 focus group interviews with 59 residents in Switzerland, with an average age of 80, to identify the competencies they possess and the skills they lack. Participants described using digital tools to stay connected and maintain autonomy. However, they also reported barriers such as cognitive limitations, rapid technological changes, and difficulty managing digital information. Despite these challenges, many expressed interest in improving their digital abilities. Our findings show that older adults in care settings want to engage with technology but often lack the necessary support. We conclude that providing hands-on training, simplifying digital interfaces, and offering ongoing assistance can reduce frustration, build confidence, and help residents manage daily tasks more independently.

records.title: Building Student Skills and Belonging as Geroscience and Gerojustice Researchers Through a Longevity and Aging Research Education Program: A Qualitative Analysis
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: Addressing cumulative health disparities across the lifespan requires a scientific workforce trained at the intersection of geroscience and gerojustice. By integrating holistic academic and social support, an interdisciplinary Longevity and Aging minor, and scaffolded intramural and extramural research mentorship, the Katies for Aging Research and Equity (KARE) Program at St. Catherine University positions students to succeed as future aging researchers. To evaluate student growth, focus group transcripts, written reflections, Individual Development Plans, and student advocacy testimonials were examined. The qualitative analysis revealed three interconnected themes defining the scholar experience: (1) scholarly skill development, (2) belonging to a scholarly community, and (3) reframing longevity and aging. Beyond individual scholar growth, the KARE program has catalyzed broader institutional shifts, driving student-led research advocacy, interdisciplinary curriculum integration, and university-wide age-friendly initiatives. We offer a model for training future researchers to address complex health disparities in the intersecting fields of geroscience and gerojustice.

records.title: Understanding Turnover Intention Among Institutional Eldercare Workers: A Structural Equation Model Based on the Conservation of Resources Theory
records.abstract: This study aimed to examine the factors influencing turnover intention among institutional eldercare workers in China, drawing upon the Conservation of Resources (COR) theory.  China’s rapid population aging and increasing years lived with disability have substantially heightened the demand for long-term care services. However, workforce shortages and high turnover rates among eldercare workers remain critical challenges.  A cross-sectional survey involving 348 caregivers from 43 institutions in Zhejiang Province employed the Maslach Burnout Inventory, Caregiver Burden Scale, and Job Satisfaction Scale. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was utilized to assess direct, mediating, and moderating relationships.  Depersonalization, diminished personal accomplishment, and job satisfaction significantly predicted turnover intention. Job satisfaction fully mediated the relationship between occupational stress and turnover intention, while colleague support amplified the adverse impact of depersonalization.

records.title: Studying What Matters: South Texas Community-Driven Dementia Research Priorities
records.abstract: South Texas has among the highest dementia prevalence rates in the United States, yet communities in the region remain consistently underrepresented in dementia research. Aligning research studies with what matters to communities most impacted by dementia is critical in addressing the crisis of research exclusion. This participatory study sought to identify community-driven dementia research priorities grounded in the experiences and needs of South Texas residents impacted by dementia. A two-year community-engaged study was conducted in partnership with a Community Council composed of individuals living with dementia, family caregivers, community health workers, and community-serving professionals. A plática program model was co-developed and implemented to elicit lived experiences with dementia and inform the development of a priority-setting survey. The resulting survey included 21 research topics grouped into four themes: (1) awareness of dementia, (2) experiences living with dementia, (3) families caring for someone living with dementia, and (4) resources to support families. Respondents ( N = 152) rated each topic on a 1–10 importance scale and selected their top two priorities by theme. Descriptive statistics were used to identify highly rated and frequently prioritized topics. Importance ratings were uniformly high across all topics (range: 8.44–9.39). Ranking data revealed clear priorities within themes wherein respondents prioritized timely diagnosis, improved provider communication, behavioral symptom management using non-pharmacological approaches, co-caregiving strategies, and system-level resources such as financial and legal planning supports. These priorities were largely consistent across respondent subgroups. The participatory approach of this study enhances the relevance of findings and demonstrates the value of community-engaged  for shaping research agendas. These community-defined priorities offer timely direction for researchers, funders, and policymakers aiming to reduce dementia disparities in South Texas and improve the equity, translational potential, and impact of future research.

records.title: Napping Characteristics and Incident Dementia: Results From The National Health and Aging Trends Study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Whether daytime napping may be a risk factor for dementia, in addition to nighttime sleep disturbances, remains unclear. This study investigated longitudinal associations of napping characteristics with incident dementia among U.S. older adults.  Data came from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS). Napping characteristics were self-reported in a sleep module at round 3 (2013), including (1) frequency (non-napper, infrequent, frequent); (2) intention (non-napper, intentional, unintentional); (3) duration (non-napper, ≤30 minutes, >30 minutes). Dementia classification was established at each round using a validated algorithm and possible/probable dementia served as our outcome. We included 995 participants free of possible/probable dementia at round 3 who were followed up to round 13 (2023). Discrete-time complementary log-log models were used for hazard ratio (HR) of incident possible/probable dementia associated with napping characteristics, adjusting for demographic, health, and sleep variables (duration, daytime sleepiness, obstructive sleep apnea risk).  When compared to non-nappers, frequent nappers had 1.48 times the hazard of developing incident possible/probable dementia (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14, 1.94). Unintentional napping was associated with incident possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.39, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.81). No associations were found for infrequent or intentional napping. Napping ≤30 minutes was associated with possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.85), but the association of napping >30 minutes was attenuated with additional adjustment for sleep variables (HR = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.96, 1.69).  Daytime napping may be a modifiable risk factor for dementia if supported by further evidence. Future studies with detailed napping characteristics and longer follow-up are needed.
